stories.author: kagaherk
stories.title: Working with AI
stories.groq_label: Companies adopt AI to increase output and reshape workflows, encountering expert resistance, bottlenecks, and modest employment impacts while emphasizing role reorganization.
stories.groq_explain:
The article reports on a study of how businesses are incorporating large‑language‑model AI into their work. Anthropic interviewed 66 people from 58 enterprise customers across a wide range of sectors, including manufacturers, technology firms, law offices, engineering firms, dentists, accountants, hedge funds and private‑equity groups. The goal was to understand where AI creates value, what obstacles companies encounter, and how they are reshaping human roles around increasingly capable models.

The researchers found that companies are applying AI to a “dizzying range” of knowledge‑work tasks. A prominent trend is the use of coding agents that let non‑technical employees add software functionality. Most respondents said AI adds value primarily by raising output rather than by cutting costs, because the technology speeds up existing work and also enables new products and services.

Regarding employment, the interviews revealed very few instances of domestic layoffs directly caused by AI automation. Some firms reported hiring more staff because of AI, but the majority said they were hiring less and were reducing reliance on contractors, especially offshore providers. The authors suggest that these reductions could foreshadow broader disruption in the international business‑services labor market.

Companies reported several bottlenecks to effective AI deployment. Expert resistance, tasks that do not speed up with AI and the need for downstream activities—such as code review, sales and strategic decision‑making—to keep pace with faster coding—were all cited as constraints. The study also examined the limits of top‑down versus bottom‑up adoption strategies. Top‑down rollouts that target a specific workflow can generate job insecurity, fears of surveillance and pushback from the experts needed to implement durable solutions. Bottom‑up distribution of tools may produce useful use cases, but it often suffers from uneven adoption and implementations that focus on single tasks only.

The highest‑value uses of AI, according to interviewees, involve purposeful reorganization of work. Some firms are expanding employee responsibilities so individuals own entire workflows, while redeploying staff to “bottleneck” tasks that AI cannot yet handle. Others are building infrastructure that supports non‑developer coding and granting broader internal access to business data. These approaches aim to capture ongoing improvements in model capabilities rather than assuming AI tools will stay at their current level.

The article illustrates these dynamics with three case studies from law firms. In the first, a simple mail‑room workflow was fully automated, improving efficiency but raising concerns about displacement of clerks. The second firm struggled with adoption bottlenecks, leading to limited productivity gains and occasional errors caused by hallucinated AI outputs. The third firm introduced AI early, used it to automate time‑keeping, and then reorganized junior lawyers to collaborate with seniors on AI‑generated drafts, preserving jobs while leveraging the technology.

Overall, the piece argues that AI’s impact on the economy will be shaped not just by the technology itself but by how organizations redesign roles, address resistance, and align human expertise with AI capabilities. Understanding these patterns is important for businesses seeking productivity gains, for policymakers monitoring labor market shifts, and for workers navigating the evolving relationship between human work and intelligent systems.

stories.author: b0m
stories.title: Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B
stories.groq_label: Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B delivers stronger agentic coding, multi‑turn tool use and faster, more accurate task execution while maintaining a 5.9 GB footprint.
stories.groq_explain:
The announcement introduces Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an upgraded version of the earlier Ternary Bonsai 2 27B model. Built on the Qwen 3.8 27B architecture, the new model keeps the same 5.9 GB footprint while delivering substantially stronger agentic coding, multi‑turn tool use, and multi‑step task execution. The improvements are aimed at developers who need on‑device agents capable of working with private files and tools, making this the strongest AI model of its size for agentic workloads.

Compared with its predecessor, Ternary Bonsai 2.5 reduces the number of interaction turns, uses fewer tokens, and provides faster, more accurate results. The release focuses on handling longer sequences of tool calls, better interpreting results, adapting when steps fail, and maintaining the overall task objective. It also addresses issues of excessive thinking and repetitive loops that were present in the earlier model, narrowing the performance gap to the full‑precision base model while retaining the compact size.

Benchmark results show marked gains over both Ternary Bonsai 2 27B and the full‑precision Qwen 3.8 27B across several tasks, including SWE‑bench, DeepSWE, Terminal‑Bench, AppWorld, τ³‑Bench, BigCodeBench, and LiveCodeBench. On a single NVIDIA H100 GPU the model generates 291 tokens per second with multi‑token processing and handles a 2,000‑token prompt at 3,200 tokens per second. On a consumer‑grade RTX 4090 it achieves 204 tokens per second and processes prompts at roughly 3,060 tokens per second.

The announcement includes a demo where the model reproduces and fixes a pytest regression, illustrating how local deployment can enable coding assistants, document summarizers, or desktop analysts that operate on private data without sending it to the cloud. The model runs on NVIDIA and Intel GPUs via llama.cpp and on Apple devices through MLX, and its weights are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Technical details about the compression, evaluation, and benchmarking methods are provided in a linked whitepaper. PrismML offers collaboration opportunities to fine‑tune the model for specific domains or optimize inference for target hardware, inviting interested parties to contact them via sales@prismml.com. The company, founded by Caltech researchers with backing from Khosla Ventures, Cerberus, Google, and Samsung, highlights its focus on compressing neural networks without losing reasoning ability and encourages applications and career inquiries through its website.

stories.author: Artgor
stories.title: From CUDA and Jax to TorchTPU: Lessons from a Cayley Graph Solver
stories.groq_label: Optimized TorchTPU matches or outperforms A100 GPU and JAX TPU implementations for a Cayley graph solver after extensive tuning
stories.groq_explain:
The post recounts the author’s experience moving a combinatorial‑puzzle solver from a GPU‑based PyTorch pipeline and a JAX implementation on TPUs to the newly released TorchTPU backend, which lets native PyTorch code run on Google’s Tensor Processing Units. The original solver, created for the CayleyPy Professor Tetraminx competition, searches for the shortest sequence of moves that resolves 1,000 scrambled puzzles. Each puzzle state is a node in a Cayley graph with 24 possible moves, and the solver uses a beam‑search guided by a 3.4‑million‑parameter transformer model (the PieceTransformer) that predicts the distance to the solved state for each possible move in a single forward pass.

Training on an Nvidia A100 GPU took about 143 seconds per epoch, and a 2,000‑epoch run required roughly 80 hours. The author’s goal was to see whether TorchTPU could match or exceed that speed while preserving solution quality. TorchTPU differs from PyTorch/XLA in that it lowers ATen operations directly to StableHLO and runs them through the TPU runtime, offering three execution modes: eager (default), fused eager (enabled with the TORCH_TPU_DEFER_AND_FUSE environment variable), and compiled (via torch.compile with static shapes). The author notes that fixed tensor shapes work best, while operations that produce data‑dependent output sizes trigger costly host round‑trips and recompilations.

The first functional port to a four‑chip v6e TPU used distributed data parallelism with a global batch size of 512, matching the sample count of the GPU run. Several GPU‑specific idioms had to be removed, such as masked‑select loss operations, boolean‑mask indexing, frequent .item() reads, and sampling of training anchors on the CPU. This initial version ran 1.65 times slower than the A100, taking 235 seconds per epoch.

Performance was improved through a series of targeted changes. Enabling fused eager execution with the TORCH_TPU_DEFER_AND_FUSE flag merged many tiny operations at runtime, cutting the data‑pipeline step from 61 ms to 13 ms per iteration and reducing overall epoch time to 176 seconds. Further gains came from rewriting the attention mechanism, eliminating dynamic tensor shapes, fixing a subtle deduplication bug, and addressing an attention‑routing regression. After these refinements the training loop ran in about 132 seconds per epoch, essentially matching the GPU baseline, and the optimized beam‑search on the same eight‑chip v6e machine became roughly 25 percent faster than the JAX implementation while achieving identical solution lengths on six test puzzles.

The investigation not only validated TorchTPU as a viable alternative to both CUDA and JAX for this type of search problem but also uncovered upstream issues that were reported to the TorchTPU repository, leading to fixes in the attention‑routing code. The author provides the full code in Kaggle notebooks that can be executed on a free TPU v5e‑8 instance. The article demonstrates that while getting TorchTPU to run is straightforward, extracting high performance requires careful attention to static shapes, eager‑mode fusion, and elimination of data‑dependent operations.

stories.author: fishcharlie
stories.title: Cloudflare hides shortcomings of the underlying infrastructure
stories.groq_label: Cloudflare masks legacy origin server connections behind modern front-end protocols, reducing transparency and delaying full internet modernization.
stories.groq_explain:
This article discusses how Cloudflare, despite driving the adoption of modern internet standards such as IPv6, TLS, and post-quantum encryption, conceals the underlying deficiencies of original web servers. While end users may enjoy a secure and modern connection to Cloudflare, the link between Cloudflare and the origin server may rely on unencrypted traffic and older networking standards. This creates a disconnect between the security and technology presented to visitors and the true state of the backend infrastructure.

A central point of the article is that Cloudflare does not adequately alert website administrators about these backend shortcomings. Website owners must actively look for this information rather than receiving clear, proactive warnings in the administrative dashboard when their origin servers fall short of modern practices. Furthermore, Cloudflare defaults to using IPv4 over IPv6 when contacting origin servers that support both protocols, effectively undermining its own efforts to promote IPv6 adoption across the web.

To address these issues, the author suggests that the web industry develop methods for content delivery networks to share origin connection data, such as encryption status and IP version, directly with users and researchers. Transparency regarding the entire connection path would hold website owners accountable for weak security practices. Ultimately, the article argues that Cloudflare should use its prominent position to encourage genuine backend modernization rather than allowing site operators to indefinitely hide outdated infrastructure behind a modern front end.

stories.author: louiereederson
stories.title: Active intrusion campaign against Check Point security management servers
stories.groq_label: Intrusion campaign identified by GreyNoise exploited multiple CVEs to compromise Check Point Security Management Servers across at least 22 global organizations.
stories.groq_explain:
GreyNoise’s Global Observation Grid, a large‑scale sensor network that attracts adversarial scanning and exploitation, identified an active intrusion campaign against Check Point Security Management Servers. The campaign, catalogued as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13), was observed from 17 October to 2 November 2026 and affected at least twenty‑two distinct organizations across a wide geographic spread that includes the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, the Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia and the United States. The victims operate in diverse sectors such as financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering and manufacturing. At present the activity has not been linked to any known threat group and the motivation behind the attacks remains unclear.

The attackers employed ninety‑nine IP addresses, many of which were disposable or routed through ExpressVPN, and also leveraged compromised Check Point devices as “operational relay boxes” or hops to forward traffic and store stolen data from twenty‑four compromised management servers. Their toolset included Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko and other Python‑based utilities, and they carried out internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation and lateral movement. Exploitation attempts targeted a range of known vulnerabilities, notably CVE‑2026‑61500 in Rejetto HFS, CVE‑2025‑5777 in Citrix NetScaler, CVE‑2024‑21893 in Ivanti, CVE‑2026‑41089 in Windows NetLogon, CVE‑2026‑16232 which bypasses authentication in Check Point SmartConsole to run scripts, and CVE‑2026‑98432 affecting Linux IPv4 handling. GreyNoise observed more than fourteen hundred network sessions, over eight hundred command‑line artifacts and more than twelve hundred files that were downloaded, uploaded or created during the campaign.

A detailed example shows how the actors automated the compromise of an HFS server. They scanned for the vulnerable service, then performed repeated logins to the loginSrp1 endpoint, collecting session cookie values generated by JavaScript’s Math.random(). By reconstructing the internal state of the V8 pseudorandom number generator, they derived the signing key for the cookies and forged an admin‑level session cookie that worked from any IP address. Using this forged cookie they logged in as an administrator, installed middleware hooks to execute commands, and appended an SSH public key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. Subsequent automated checks executed system commands such as “uname ‑a”, “df ‑h”, and “whoami”. Later, on 19 October, the actors established the operational relay box, reusing the compromised server as a hop for further activity.

Although direct observation of the campaign ceased after 2 November, the presence of persistent access to Check Point devices suggests that the intrusion is ongoing. GreyNoise is cooperating with international government partners and computer‑security incident response teams to share intelligence and alert affected organizations. The report underscores the sophistication of the threat, the importance of rapid patching for the cited CVEs, and the need for continuous monitoring of security‑management infrastructure to detect and mitigate similar multi‑stage attacks.

stories.author: zdw
stories.title: Jetty Pro
stories.groq_label: AI-assisted development finally produced a niche Mac app that offers a customizable corner folder palette.
stories.groq_explain:
The article is a personal narrative about the author’s long‑term effort to recreate and improve features that were lost when the Mac app DragThing was retired in 2019. The author first built two small utilities, Front and Center and SwitchGlass, to bring back a single checkbox option and a specific floating palette from DragThing. Over the years the author added more niche apps, including Hyperspace, which reclaimed disk space without deleting files and demonstrated a broader appeal beyond DragThing‑style tools.

A persistent annoyance for the author has been the inability to have a simple, permanent folder palette in a screen corner, something DragThing offered. The author experimented with adding that feature to SwitchGlass but never released it, feeling it did not belong in the app. The rise of AI coding agents sparked a renewed attempt: the author fed the SwitchGlass source code to an AI, asking it to modernize the SwiftUI implementation and support multiple palettes. The AI produced a functional but rough version, which the author then refined over several months.

During this process the author realized the project had grown into a full replacement for the macOS Dock, a component the author has long found limiting. Specific frustrations include the Dock’s change in 2009 that requires a Command‑Option click to open a folder, the lack of notification badges, date display, bouncing icons, and quit actions in third‑party dock replacements. Because the Dock is a privileged part of the operating system, sandboxed Mac App Store apps cannot replicate its full behavior, whereas unsandboxed apps can use private APIs.

To explore the limits, the author announced a plan on the Accidental Tech Podcast to create two versions of a new dock replacement: Jetty, which would be sold through the Mac App Store and remain sandboxed, and Jetty Pro, an unsandboxed version distributed directly to customers. While developing both, the author found the plain Jetty version to be lacking compared to the more powerful Jetty Pro. The article stops before describing Jetty Pro’s final feature set, but it makes clear that Jetty Pro is intended to be a more capable, unrestricted dock replacement that can implement the missing behaviors the author has missed for years. The piece matters because it illustrates how AI‑assisted development can enable niche, highly customized macOS utilities that were previously considered too costly to build, and it highlights the trade‑offs between App Store sandboxing and the deeper system integration possible with unsandboxed software.

stories.author: bluepeter
stories.title: A training engine for your local model, using your idle compute
stories.groq_label: Songe uses idle compute resources to locally train AI models based on past interactions and corrections.
stories.groq_explain:
Songe is an open-source local model training engine licensed under Apache-2.0. It runs entirely on a user's local machine, leveraging idle compute power to personalize and improve local artificial intelligence models without sending data to the cloud. Songe sits between local AI agents, such as opencode or pi, and local model servers, such as LM Studio, vLLM, Ollama, llama.cpp, or mlx-lm. As users interact with their AI tools, Songe acts as a local proxy, recording conversation context, user corrections, stated rules, retries, and tool execution errors.

The system improves models through two primary idle background processes referred to as Dreams. A Quick Dream takes a few minutes and updates the model's instructions with stated user preferences. A Deep Dream takes an hour or more and actively trains a small adapter on the model. During Deep Dreams, Songe uses on-policy distillation where short practice scenes are generated based on identified lessons, allowing the model to practice without directly training on raw user conversations. Rehearsal techniques are also included to ensure previous skills are retained.

Safety, validation, and privacy are central to the software's design. Songe automatically evaluates trained versions by running comparative tests against past user interactions. A newly trained version is adopted only if it demonstrates clear improvements without regressing on existing capabilities or producing unhealthy output. If a model update is unsatisfactory, users can instantly revert to any earlier version. The software operates entirely locally with no account creation, telemetry, cloud services, or external tool execution, keeping all data securely on the user's computer.

Hardware and system requirements vary based on functionality. Serving and recording interactions can run on machines without dedicated graphics processors, but actual training requires supported hardware such as Apple Silicon using MLX, or NVIDIA and AMD hardware using PyTorch. Installation is handled through tools like uv, pipx, or Homebrew across macOS, Linux, and Windows. The application includes a command-line interface and a web dashboard for managing settings, toggling automatic training, checking system health, and inspecting model performance.

Songe matters because it provides a private, automated way to continually adapt open-source local language models to individual workflows, preferences, and tool environments using existing local hardware during downtime.

stories.author: fcjr
stories.title: Splitting USB-C: USB 3 and USB 2 on one port
stories.groq_label: Directly passing through USB 3 signals while using USB 2 lines on the same USB-C port enables simultaneous high-speed data transfer and microcontroller control.
stories.groq_explain:
This article describes the design and testing of Dongle-Pro v2, a custom hardware adapter created for restoring Apple Mac computers. The author previously built inline USB-C adapters called restorekit dongles, which sit between a host computer and a target Mac. These devices trigger Apple's lowest-level recovery mode, known as Device Firmware Update or DFU mode, by sending vendor-defined commands over the USB Power Delivery protocol on the USB-C CC line. The original version, Dongle-Lite, operated purely over USB 2 using a CH334F hub and a PD PHY chip.

When the author learned that newer Macs support USB 3 speeds for recovery operations, they set out to upgrade the dongle to enable faster restores. The initial design, Dongle-Pro v1, used a standard GL3510 USB 3 hub chip paired with Texas Instruments SuperSpeed multiplexers. This design was expensive and bulky, more than doubling the component count and bill-of-materials cost to over ten dollars while limiting transfer speeds to 5 Gbps.

To make a cheaper and smaller board, the author took advantage of how USB-C is structured. A single physical USB-C port is not a single combined bus, but is internally connected to two separate root ports on the computer host controller: one for USB 2 using the central D+ and D- pins, and another for USB 3 using dedicated high-speed SuperSpeed lanes on the outer edges.

In the updated Dongle-Pro v2 design, the author removed the USB 3 hub chip entirely. The USB 2 signals are routed to a low-cost CH334P hub that handles the dongle microcontroller unit and standard USB 2 pass-through to the target. The USB 3 SuperSpeed lanes bypass the hub completely and act as a direct pass-through between the host and target. Two cheap CH9441P multiplexer chips monitor cable orientation on each end and route the active high-speed lanes straight to each other across a short board corridor without any hub or active redriver chip.

Despite concerns regarding signal loss across passive multiplexers without a redriver, potential interference with the USB Power Delivery PHY on the CC lines, or host operating system drivers failing to recognize split buses, the prototype functioned as intended. The board achieved full 10 Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2 data rates while simultaneously operating the USB 2 hub and microcontroller. The total bill-of-materials cost dropped to two dollars and ninety-three cents, and the board size was reduced to twenty-one by forty-eight millimeters.

This project demonstrates that hardware developers can exploit the architectural separation of USB 2 and USB 3 within USB-C to route high-speed USB 3 data directly through a device while maintaining low-speed control interfaces over USB 2, achieving maximum transfer speeds at a fraction of the cost of dedicated USB 3 hub silicon.

stories.author: setheron
stories.title: 2035 came early
stories.groq_label: Browser‑based Linux compiled to WebAssembly now boots any Nix GUI package instantly, proving JavaScript’s dominance as a universal runtime
stories.groq_explain:
The article announces that the site trynix.dev now can start graphical Linux programs directly in a web browser. It explains that the author was inspired by Gary Bernhardt’s talk “The Birth & Death of JavaScript,” which predicts that JavaScript will eventually dominate all software, a view captured by Jeff Atwood’s law that any application that can be written in JavaScript will eventually be written in JavaScript. The talk uses a fictional look‑back from the year 2035 to describe how JavaScript would become the default language for everything. The author notes that large language models have accelerated this timeline, so the scenario described for 2035 has already arrived in 2026.

The technical breakthrough behind trynix.dev is the use of unkernel.dev, a project that compiles the Linux kernel and system components to WebAssembly. This allows the kernel to run at native WebAssembly speed while only user‑space programs are emulated. Compared with the earlier QEMU‑Wasm approach, unkernel delivers speed improvements ranging from two to thirty‑two times depending on the workload, especially on first runs where kernel work dominates. The author provides benchmark data showing dramatic reductions in start‑up time.

With unkernel, trynix.dev can launch any Nix package – over three hundred thousand distinct versions – from the browser. It supports a full Wayland desktop, networking, audio, and minimal graphics via a Mesa build compiled to WebAssembly and rendered through the browser’s WebGL2. Typical commands such as curl, git clone, and pip install work, with network traffic routed through a WebSocket to a Wisp relay.

To illustrate the power of the platform, the author describes nesting a full Firefox instance inside another Firefox tab, which in turn runs a Linux‑compiled‑to‑WebAssembly version of Firefox. The inner browser required the JIT compiler to be disabled, the middle instance ran without GL, and the outer page used a Wisp relay. The whole process took more than four hours but demonstrates that a complete graphical Linux environment can run inside a browser tab.

The article concludes that the vision of 2035 – a world where JavaScript and WebAssembly power every software layer – has arrived early, and that trynix.dev combined with unkernel shows how the web can become a practical operating system platform for running GUI applications directly in the browser. This matters because it blurs the line between native and web software, simplifies distribution, and showcases the performance potential of WebAssembly‑based kernels.

stories.author: thisislife2
stories.title: India's opposition storms Meta's offices to get its Instagram accounts back
stories.groq_label: Opposition youth wing protests forced Meta to restore blocked Instagram accounts in India
stories.groq_explain:
The article reports that activists from the Indian Youth Congress, the youth wing of the main opposition party, forcibly entered Meta’s office building in Hyderabad on a Friday, leading to clashes with police and overturned potted plants. A similar incident occurred the same day in Mumbai, where anti‑Meta slogans were spray‑painted on the building, placards were burned at the entrance, and in Gurugram near New Delhi banners were displayed demanding the restoration of the group’s Instagram accounts. Mumbai police filed complaints against four leaders of the organization and detained several protesters.

The protests were triggered by Meta’s blocking of Instagram accounts on November 19 belonging to the youth wing’s president and a party official. The Congress party alleges that Meta is acting on orders from the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and that the platform has also restricted thousands of accounts belonging to journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government. The Youth Congress warned on X that it would storm Meta offices across the country if the accounts were not reinstated, and the warning was carried out.

The protests appear to have achieved a partial result: two of the blocked accounts were restored the following day, according to the group’s social media chief, who then gave Meta a seven‑day deadline to lift all restrictions targeting opposition voices. The article notes that Meta restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India in the first half of 2026, a dramatic increase from about 70 000 in the entire previous year. In the same period the Indian government issued nearly 200 000 blocking orders and, since February, has required platforms to remove flagged content within three hours, down from the previous 36‑hour window.

India remains Meta’s largest market by user numbers, and the article suggests that the company’s increased compliance may be an effort to protect that core business. A BJP spokesperson accused the protesters of vandalising the Hyderabad office and bragging about it on social media, while Meta has not issued a comment, caught between governmental orders and opposition pressure. The piece cites The Verge as its source and notes that the article was originally written in French and automatically translated.

stories.author: zdw
stories.title: AMD EPYC Zen 6 vs. Zen 1 Performance: 12.1x Geo Mean in Less Than 10 Years
stories.groq_label: Zen 6 EPYC processors provide over twelvefold performance improvement compared to the original Zen 1 EPYC 7601 within a decade.
stories.groq_explain:
The article reports on the release of AMD’s new EPYC 9006 “Venice” SP7 processors based on the Zen 6 micro‑architecture and quantifies how much server performance has improved since the first‑generation EPYC “Naples” Zen 1 chips launched nearly ten years ago. The author uses the original EPYC 7601 Naples platform – a dual‑socket Dell PowerEdge R7425 equipped with 32 × 32 GB DDR4‑2666 memory and a Samsung SSD – as a baseline and compares it to two current Zen 6 configurations: the flagship EPYC 9996 with 256 Zen 6C cores (512 threads), 2.55 GHz base and 4.1 GHz boost clocks, 1 GB of L3 cache, 16 channels of DDR5‑RDIMM/12800 MT/s memory, 96 PCIe 6.0 lanes and a 600 W TDP, and the frequency‑optimized EPYC 9686F with 96 Zen 5 cores (192 threads), a 4.05 GHz base and up to 5.3 GHz boost, 384 MB L3 cache and also a 600 W TDP. Both newer servers were built with 32 × 64 GB DDR5‑12800 MRDIMMs and a Micron PCIe Gen 6 SSD.

All systems ran the same software stack: Ubuntu 26.10 with the Linux 7.3 kernel and GCC 15.3, allowing a direct comparison of raw performance, power draw, and performance‑per‑watt using the CPUs’ RAPL power‑cap sensors. The testing covered a broad set of real‑world workloads, and the results showed a geometric‑mean performance increase of roughly twelve‑fold (12.1×) for Zen 6 over Zen 1, while also delivering substantial efficiency gains despite the higher power envelope of the new chips.

The article highlights that the dramatic improvement is not just due to higher core counts and clock speeds, but also architectural advances introduced across the Zen generations, such as AVX‑512 support in Zen 4 (refined in Zen 5), enhanced security features that reduce reliance on software mitigations, and many other micro‑architectural refinements. These advances, combined with modern DDR5 memory and PCIe 6.0 I/O, illustrate how AMD has transformed its server offering in a decade, turning the EPYC platform from a competitive newcomer into a leader that now significantly outpaces its original generation in both speed and efficiency. This matters to data‑center operators and enterprise customers because it demonstrates the potential ROI of upgrading to the latest EPYC hardware, offering far greater compute density, lower cost per unit of work, and better power utilization.

stories.author: andai
stories.title: Making a dumb TV just smart enough
stories.groq_label: An ESP32‑based IR controller lets a TV remote launch and manage desktop media and emulator sessions, turning a basic TV into a smart entertainment hub
stories.groq_explain:
The article describes how the author transformed a basic, non‑smart television into a convenient, multi‑purpose media hub by using a small custom controller built with an ESP32‑C3 Mini board. The TV, which only had an HDMI connection to the author’s desktop computer, originally required the author to manually switch monitors, launch applications, move windows, and use a wireless keyboard to start playback, which involved a lot of unnecessary movement. To eliminate this friction, the author added an infrared transmitter and receiver, captured the TV remote’s RC‑5 codes, and programmed the ESP32 to trigger a series of scripts that automatically prepared the desktop for media playback with a single button press.

After the initial automation succeeded, the author expanded the system to launch various retro‑gaming emulators (DuckStation, PCSX2, Dolphin, Cemu, ES‑DE) and to switch between different modes such as a fireplace video loop and Steam’s Big Picture interface. By assigning additional remote buttons to these modes, the remote could start the appropriate emulator or media source without further interaction. To avoid window‑placement problems on the dual‑screen setup, the author moved to a multiseat configuration with two independent X sessions, one per screen, allowing both displays to operate simultaneously without interference.

The solution also includes a virtual remote interface that synchronizes volume changes made on the physical remote, a virtual gamepad, and a real‑time screen stream that supports mouse clicks. Connecting an Xbox controller automatically selects the relevant emulator or Steam mode, while disconnecting it returns the TV to the fireplace display. The entire project took roughly ten hours to assemble, most of which was spent configuring the emulators. While the author notes that the AI assistant (Claude) used to generate scripts sometimes produced incorrect suggestions and needed careful supervision, it significantly reduced the effort required to achieve the final setup. The article illustrates a practical, low‑cost approach to extending the functionality of an otherwise dumb TV, demonstrating how modest hardware and simple scripting can streamline home entertainment workflows.

stories.author: DeepLogin
stories.title: New York Bans Subscription and Post-Purchase Fees on Cars
stories.groq_label: New York law bans manufacturers and dealers from charging subscription or post‑purchase fees for pre‑installed vehicle features.
stories.groq_explain:
The article announces that Governor Kathy Hochul has signed a bill that bars motor‑vehicle manufacturers, dealers, and third‑party service providers from charging subscription fees or post‑purchase fees for built‑in vehicle features that do not involve an ongoing cost. The law, identified as S.9348A/A.10411A, targets practices where owners must pay recurring charges to activate functions such as heated seats, enhanced navigation, hands‑free driving, entertainment options, remote start and other pre‑installed hardware. It is intended to stop what officials describe as exploitative “junk fees” that increase the cost of living for New Yorkers.

Governor Hochul framed the measure as a response to rising consumer prices and a “Trump’s affordability crisis,” emphasizing that car owners should not have to pay extra for features already included in their purchase. Attorney General Letitia James highlighted the state’s efforts to recover illegal fees from consumers, while State Senator James Skoufis and Assemblymember William B. Magnarelli stressed that the law protects drivers from having to subscribe to features they have already paid for. The legislation will become effective 90 days after February 27, 2027.

The article places the new law within a broader agenda of Governor Hochul’s policies aimed at lowering costs for residents. It references recent actions such as reforms to reduce auto‑insurance premiums, requirements for businesses to notify consumers about renewals and price changes, cuts to middle‑class taxes, an expansion of the Child Tax Credit, free school meals for all students, inflation‑refund checks, and increased unemployment benefits. The significance of the bill lies in its attempt to curb a growing trend in the automotive industry of monetizing software features after a vehicle is sold, thereby protecting consumers from unexpected ongoing expenses.

stories.author: shaunpud
stories.title: Stalwart is now a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange
stories.groq_label: Stalwart 1.2.0 implements Exchange protocols, enabling it to serve as a drop in on premises replacement for Microsoft Exchange.
stories.groq_explain:
Stalwart 1.2.0 is being released as a direct, drop‑in replacement for Microsoft Exchange, allowing existing Exchange clients such as Outlook, Apple Mail and mobile mail apps to connect without any change in user workflow. The new version implements the full set of protocols that Exchange servers normally expose: MAPI over HTTP, Exchange Web Services, Exchange ActiveSync and Autodiscover. Because these protocols are served on the same HTTPS port as Stalwart’s JMAP interface and WebUI, a mailbox can be migrated to Stalwart, DNS records updated, and users continue to log in with their email address and password while the client automatically discovers the server.

The announcement also explains the context that makes the replacement relevant. On‑premises Exchange Server is effectively being phased out: Exchange 2016 and 2019 lost support in October 2025, the Extended Security Update program ended in October 2026, and the only supported on‑premises edition, Exchange Server Subscription Edition, receives no new features and is not compatible with the new Outlook for Windows. Microsoft is shifting all new functionality to cloud‑only APIs such as Microsoft Graph, and Exchange Web Services in Exchange Online will be retired by April 2027. These moves leave administrators with a choice between running an unsupported legacy server or moving to Microsoft’s cloud, which many organizations cannot accept due to data‑sovereignty concerns and the reach of US laws such as the CLOUD Act.

A major barrier to leaving Exchange has traditionally been the client side, because many users rely on Outlook’s deep integration for mail, calendars, contacts, delegation and shared mailboxes. Replacing Exchange with generic IMAP or CalDAV servers usually forces a change of client or a loss of functionality, which can halt migration projects. Stalwart’s implementation removes this obstacle by providing complete protocol compatibility, so Outlook (both Windows and Mac versions) and other native clients can operate exactly as they would with a real Exchange server.

Supported protocols include the native MAPI over HTTP stack for classic Outlook, covering mail, calendars, contacts, tasks, notes, address lists, delegate access, shared mailboxes and related features. The Exchange Web Services implementation supports schema versions from Exchange 2010 SP2 through Exchange 2016, handling mail, calendars, contacts, tasks, folder sharing, free/busy, inbox rules, out‑of‑office, distribution lists and notifications. Exchange ActiveSync is supported at version 14.1 and 16.1, providing push mail, calendar sync, contacts, tasks, notes, meeting responses and search. Autodiscover works in POX, SOAP and JSON forms, enabling automatic client configuration.

The range of compatible clients includes classic Outlook for Windows (2016 and later, including Microsoft 365 Apps) using MAPI over HTTP or EWS, Outlook for Mac via EWS, Apple Mail, Calendar and Contacts on macOS via EWS, iPhone and iPad mail, calendar and contacts via ActiveSync, Android mail apps that support Exchange accounts such as Gmail, Samsung Email and Nine, and Thunderbird with its built‑in EWS support or TbSync for calendar synchronization.

By providing full Exchange protocol support in an open‑source, AGPL‑licensed Community edition, Stalwart offers organizations a way to retain their existing client ecosystem while moving away from Microsoft’s on‑premises and cloud Exchange offerings, preserving data sovereignty and avoiding vendor lock‑in. This makes the release significant for enterprises, public administrations, healthcare providers, law firms, defence contractors and any European or privacy‑sensitive organization seeking an on‑premises mail solution that does not rely on US‑based cloud services.

stories.author: Dylan1312
stories.title: Levent Alpöge comments on his Riemann Hypothesis proof
stories.groq_label: Mathematician Levent Alpöge clarifies exaggerated claims about his Riemann Hypothesis proof length and responds to criticisms of the accompanying Lean code.
stories.groq_explain:
This text is a statement by mathematician Levent Alpöge addressing public reactions, misunderstandings, and criticism surrounding his work and Lean formalization regarding the Riemann Hypothesis.

Alpöge clarifies that his previous claim of a paper spanning over 250,000 pages was entirely a joke. He explains that he finds absurdly large numbers funny and attempted to signal the humor through intentionally pedantic mathematical phrasing, but people took the claim literally. Reflecting on advice from mathematician Terence Tao, he acknowledges why one should avoid putting jokes or pop culture references into academic papers. He notes that he turned to Lean formalization to avoid publishing a rushed or unreadable writeup, though he admits that the actual Lean code is messy and contains unnecessary clutter, accepting full responsibility for not cleaning it up.

Beyond correcting the record, Alpöge discusses his overall philosophy on the problem. He anticipates that the current work contains a lot of unnecessary elements that will eventually be simplified. Crucially, he argues that intense mathematical fighting over complex arguments is primarily valuable as a raw input to help construct better mathematical definitions. He suggests that the Riemann Hypothesis should ultimately be straightforward, and that the present conceptual difficulty indicates that current mathematical frameworks, such as missing an H^1 object over number fields, are still inadequate.

stories.author: mikeryan52
stories.title: VP ≠ VNP over Every Field
stories.groq_label: VP is strictly smaller than VNP over all fields and VNP is not contained in the closure of VP
stories.groq_explain:
The repository presents a claim that the algebraic complexity class VP is a proper subset of VNP over every field, and that VNP is not contained in the closure of VP. The central technical statement is that for any field, any arithmetic circuit that computes the Hamiltonian‑cycle polynomial, and any circuit that computes the permanent when the field’s characteristic is not two, must use more than m to the power of a constant times (log m) to the one‑third for all sufficiently large m. The same lower bound is asserted for circuits that approximate these polynomials. These lower bounds imply the separation VP ≠ VNP and also show that VNP does not lie in the topological closure of VP, although the result does not resolve the classic P versus NP question.

The work was generated by an internal research model named Claude from Anthropic. Both the research paper and a formal verification in the Lean 4 proof assistant were written by AI models, and no human mathematician has yet checked the correctness of the proofs. The repository contains the PDF of the paper, which includes the full proof in an appendix, and a Lean formalization consisting of several files. The file Statement.lean encodes the main statements and imports only Mathlib; it is intended to be checked by Lean, though the repository notes that the file does not itself guarantee that the formal statements correspond exactly to the informal claims. The file Challenge.lean contains the theorems without proofs for a fuller consistency check. Build instructions using the elan tool and lake commands are provided, and a CI script runs a comparator that cross‑checks the statements against Challenge.lean and re‑verifies the proofs with an independent kernel called nanoda. The build process should produce no axioms other than the logical foundations propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound.

The repository is labeled as a research artifact, is not maintained, and is not accepting contributions. It is released under the Apache 2.0 license, with licensing details in the LICENSE and NOTICE files.

stories.title: GPUI is getting its own repository
stories.groq_label: GPUI is being moved to a standalone repository.

Based on the title and the available text, it can be inferred that GPUI, the GPU-accelerated user interface framework originally built for the Zed text editor, is being separated into its own dedicated code repository. The reference to crates.io indicates that GPUI is written in Rust and is intended for distribution as an independent Rust library. The brief placeholder message suggests that the repository setup or code migration is currently in progress and will be fully available shortly. 

This change matters because separating GPUI into its own repository allows Rust developers to use the framework to build high-performance, GPU-accelerated graphical user interfaces for their own standalone applications without needing to import the entire Zed editor codebase.

stories.author: tech234a
stories.title: Per Arm's request, this site will be discontinued on 4 December 2026 :(
stories.groq_label: An Arm architecture reference documentation site will shut down on December 4 2026 due to legal action from Arm.
stories.groq_explain:
This page announces that the website arm.jonpalmisc.com will be permanently discontinued on December 4, 2026. The creator, Jon, explains that this shutdown is taking place because Arm's legal team instructed him to remove the site or face legal action. Jon expresses gratitude to the user community, including fans of the site inside Arm itself, for their support over the years, and mentions that he hopes to find a solution to keep existing bookmarks and links working after the site goes offline.

The website serves as an independent reference documentation resource for the AArch64 instruction set and system registers defined by the Armv8-A and Armv9-A architectures. It allows users to search for or manually browse listings of instructions, including Base, SIMD, SVE, and SME, as well as AArch64 and AArch32 system registers. The site utilizes WebAssembly to power its search features.

This notice matters because it marks the end of a popular, user-friendly documentation resource that many developers relied on for Arm architecture specifications, highlighting the impact of legal enforcement by hardware companies on community-created developer tools.

stories.title: Ladybird is now in alpha
stories.groq_label: Ladybird, a new browser built on a proprietary engine, is now available in alpha for macOS and Linux.
stories.groq_explain: The post announces that Ladybird, a new web browser with its own independently built engine, has reached an alpha release that can be downloaded for macOS and Linux. The author explains that the engine is not a fork of an existing project and that the surrounding browser is modest but functional. As an alpha version, some websites may not work correctly and crashes are expected; users are encouraged to report broken sites and optionally send crash reports, with details provided in the privacy policy. The developers invite security researchers to test and attempt to compromise the browser, asking that any successful attacks be reported so the team can improve security. Updates will be delivered automatically through a rolling channel, allowing rapid improvements without requiring users to build the software from source. Web developers are asked to test their sites in Ladybird and report any issues, and the browser supports WebDriver for automated testing as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol. The announcement concludes with thanks to sponsors, donors, testers, bug reporters, and contributors, and acknowledges that a substantial amount of work remains before the project is complete. This matters because it makes a new, self‑developed browser engine publicly available for testing, inviting community participation in both functional and security aspects of its development.

stories.author: jaz
stories.title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
stories.groq_label: Nvidia board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, citing no national security risk and prompting a sharp stock rise.
stories.groq_explain:
Nvidia announced on Monday that Jensen Huang has been reinstated as chief executive officer, effective immediately, after a brief period in which he had resigned following revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, including a relationship with a woman identified as Alice Huang who was reported to have been in contact with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security. The board of directors voted unanimously to restore Huang after a series of discussions and meetings, stating that it had received input from senior levels of the United States government and that his return posed no national security risk.  

President Donald Trump told CNBC that he had spoken directly and indirectly with Nvidia’s board and with Huang, affirming that Huang had done nothing wrong and urging him to work hard. Trump posted on his social‑media platform that the board made “the correct and proper decision” and described Huang as a “great patriot and national treasure.” Several technology leaders, including Elon Musk, Gavin Baker and Brad Gerstner, publicly supported Huang’s return.  

Nvidia’s shares rose sharply, closing up 31 percent after the announcement, recovering from a roughly 33‑percent decline that began when Huang first admitted to an affair on November 8. In a statement, Huang expressed humility and renewed commitment to leading the company during what he called a new industrial revolution.  

The board’s decision was influenced in part by concerns about the company’s collapsing stock price. After Huang’s ouster, the board appointed CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, a role she retained after filing a Securities and Exchange Commission document. An independent committee and the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz were tasked with investigating whether any company secrets or national security matters had been compromised. The board said the investigation would continue to its conclusion and that Huang would cooperate.  

Despite Huang’s reinstatement, Nvidia continues to face heightened scrutiny over its chip sales in Southeast Asia and China. Lawmakers are preparing investigations into whether Huang’s alleged affair with a Chinese spy affected U.S. AI dominance, export‑control positions, and his relationships with the Trump administration. Senator Elizabeth Warren criticized the decision, stating that the company still owes Congress answers about compliance with export controls. Huang is scheduled for a closed‑door interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on December 1, and general counsel Tim Teter will appear before the panels on December 2.  

Overall, the article details the rapid reversal of Huang’s resignation, the political and regulatory context surrounding the decision, the immediate positive market reaction, and the ongoing legal and congressional scrutiny that Nvidia must address.

stories.author: surprisetalk
stories.title: An Italian folding bicycle design that fits into a suitcase
stories.groq_label: The 1963 T&C Pocket Bici is an Italian bicycle designed to fold entirely into its own frame and fit inside a suitcase.
stories.groq_explain:
The article showcases the T&C Pocket Bici, a historical folding bicycle designed and built in 1963 by the Italian metalworking firm Tresoldi & Casiraghi. Unlike many modern folding bicycles that collapse by splitting the frame in half, this vintage design allows all of the bicycle's components to fold neatly into its central, racetrack-shaped frame. Once fully collapsed, the entire vehicle fits completely inside its own dedicated carrying suitcase.

The origin and commercial history of the bicycle remain somewhat unclear due to conflicting accounts. One auction source claims that the bicycle was developed specifically for the Chinese market and that 2,500 units were ultimately sold. Conversely, a platform called BikeFlip reports that a group in China placed an order for 2,000 units, but after the Italian manufacturer produced the first 1,000 bicycles, payment was never received, causing the overall project to be cancelled.

Despite the uncertainty surrounding its full production run, visual evidence suggests that at least some of the bicycles were distributed to their intended market. A video showing the bike being unfurled originates from a Chinese video channel, confirming that some units made it to China. The T&C Pocket Bici matters as a notable mid-twentieth-century engineering attempt to create an exceptionally portable, self-contained bicycle for compact travel and storage.
